hook: A single figure turns thought itself into sculpture.
summary_en: A serene gilt-bronze bodhisattva whose crossed leg, lowered gaze, and slight smile have become an emblem of Korean Buddhist art.
summary_ko: 반가의 자세, 내려앉은 시선, 미소가 한국 불교조각의 상징이 된 금동 보살상입니다.

sections.why_this_matters: For visitors new to Korean art, this is the quietest possible monument: not a ruler, not a weapon, but concentration made visible.
sections.what_you_are_looking_at: The bodhisattva sits with one leg folded over the other and one hand lifted toward the cheek, a posture associated with contemplative images of Maitreya. The body is spare rather than ornamental: a simple crown, exposed torso, and balanced proportions keep attention on the face and hand.
sections.the_story: Such pensive images moved across East Asia with Buddhism, but Korea gave the type an unusually inward mood. National Treasure No. 83 is often compared with the red-pine bodhisattva at Kōryūji in Kyoto, a reminder that sculpture, belief, and technique crossed the sea long before modern borders.
